claim: "The bass side (called the dagga) is struck with a thick wooden stick to produce a deep, resonant boom. The treble side (called the tilli) is struck with a thin, curved cane stick..." Repeated in flashcard_questions ("struck on the bass side (dagga) with a thick stick and on the treble side (tilli) with a thin cane stick") and in the practice_questions mark scheme for "Describe how the dhol produces two contrasting sounds from one instrument" ("the bass side (dagga) struck with a thick stick... the treble side (tilli) struck with a thin cane stick").
problem: Dagga and tilli (also spelled tihai/thili/chanti) are the names of the two STICKS used to play the dhol, not the names of the drum's two skins/sides. Multiple sources (chandrakantha.com, ohmydhol.co.uk) confirm the sides themselves are simply called the bass side and treble side, with the dagga (thicker, bent/curved at the striking end) used to hit the bass side and the tilli/chanti (thinner, straight cane) used to hit the treble side. The lesson also reverses which stick is curved: sources describe the dagga as the curved stick and the tilli/chanti as straight, but the lesson calls the tilli "curved" and leaves the dagga's shape undescribed.
correction: Dagga = the thick, curved wooden stick that strikes the bass side. Tilli (or tihai/chanti) = the thin, straight cane stick that strikes the treble side. The drum's two skins are simply the "bass side" and "treble side" — they do not carry the dagga/tilli names themselves.

claim: H2 heading "The Drum Groove: Jeff Porcaro's Half-Time Shuffle" and surrounding text: "combining a shuffle feel (a swung, triplet-based subdivision) with a half-time backbeat"; also knowledge_checks ("What term describes Jeff Porcaro's drum groove in 'Africa'?" → correct answer "Half-time shuffle"), a flashcard, the glossary term "Half-time shuffle", two practice_questions with mark schemes requiring the term, and exam_tip_html which specifically warns against "describing the half-time shuffle groove as simply 'a drum beat'".
problem: "Half-time shuffle" (also called the "Rosanna shuffle") is the name given to the swung, triplet-based groove Jeff Porcaro created for Toto's OTHER Toto IV track, 'Rosanna' — combining the Purdie shuffle, John Bonham's 'Fool in the Rain' pattern and the Bo Diddley beat. Porcaro's own documented description of the 'Africa' groove is different: "The backbeat is on 3, so it's a half-time feel, and it's 16th notes on the hi-hat" — a straight (not shuffled/swung) 16th-note hi-hat pattern with a subtle accent, plus congas from percussionist Lenny Castro. No source calls Africa's groove a "shuffle". The lesson has conflated the two songs' drum grooves.
correction: Describe Africa's groove as a "half-time" feel only (backbeat placed on beat 3 rather than the usual 2 and 4), played as straight 16th notes on the hi-hat with a distinctive accent, layered with congas/percussion (Lenny Castro). Either drop the word "shuffle" throughout, or explicitly note that the true "half-time shuffle"/"Rosanna shuffle" (swung/triplet feel) belongs to 'Rosanna', a different track on the same album, not to 'Africa'.
field: content_html, knowledge_checks, flashcard_questions, glossary_terms, practice_questions, exam_tip_html

claim: Both embedded-video captions in content_html: "Watch: the official video. Listen for the layered keyboards, the half-time shuffle groove and the lifted chorus harmony."
problem: Same "half-time shuffle" mislabelling as Lesson 3 — this term describes the groove on Toto's 'Rosanna', not 'Africa'. See the Lesson 3 finding for sourcing (Jeff Porcaro's own description of the Africa groove: "half-time feel... 16th notes on the hi-hat", no shuffle/swing).
correction: Change both captions to something like "the half-time drum groove" (drop "shuffle").

claim: "The track opens with a bright, repeating melodic pattern that imitates the sound of an African kalimba (thumb piano). This is not an acoustic instrument at all — it is created using a digital synthesizer..." Repeated in the knowledge_checks answer ("A programmed synthesizer") and a flashcard ("A digital synthesizer programmed with a fast decay... to imitate a plucked, metallic, percussive sound").
problem: This overstates the case. Steve Porcaro did programme and multi-layer (six tracks) a Yamaha GS-1 digital synthesizer to imitate a kalimba, but independent sources describe the finished intro as the GS-1 pattern "with accompaniment from a marimba" — i.e. a real acoustic marimba is also layered in. The flat claim that the sound is "not an acoustic instrument at all" is not fully supported, and it directly contradicts Lesson 4, which describes the same ostinato as being played on "marimba and kalimba".
correction: State that the intro pattern is a layered blend: a Yamaha GS-1 synthesizer programmed and multi-tracked to imitate a kalimba, combined with a real acoustic marimba part — rather than asserting the sound is "not acoustic at all".

claim: "'Africa' opens with a marimba and kalimba (thumb piano) ostinato... The verse adds bass guitar, drum kit and keyboard chords over the marimba ostinato"; knowledge_checks ("What instrument provides the continuous ostinato pattern in 'Africa'?" → "Marimba/kalimba"); flashcard ("Marimba (with kalimba/thumb piano), heard from the introduction onward").
problem: No literal kalimba (thumb piano) is played on the recording — the kalimba-like sound is a Yamaha GS-1 synthesizer programmed and multi-layered to imitate one (see the Lesson 3 finding). Describing the ostinato as simply "marimba and kalimba" instruments omits the synthesizer that most sources treat as the track's single most famous production detail, and contradicts Lesson 3's own claim that the sound is purely synthetic.
correction: Describe the ostinato as a layered combination of a programmed/multi-tracked Yamaha GS-1 synthesizer (imitating a kalimba) and a real acoustic marimba part, rather than as literal marimba-plus-kalimba instruments.

claim: "Later in the song there is an instrumental synthesizer solo, played on the kind of analogue/digital hybrid synthesizers (such as the Yamaha CS-80 and GX-1)..."
problem: No reliable source documents a Yamaha GX-1 being used on 'Africa'. Multiple independent sources (Reverb News, Vintage Synth Explorer forums, Wikipedia, Stereogum) confirm the two synths used on the track are the Yamaha CS-80 (played by David Paich for the synth "call" figure/lead line) and the Yamaha GS-1 (used for the kalimba-imitating ostinato). The GX-1 is a different, extremely rare and expensive Yamaha instrument ($60,000, used by acts like Stevie Wonder) with no documented connection to this recording — this looks like a name mix-up between GS-1 and GX-1.
correction: Remove "GX-1". The synth solo/lead line was played on the Yamaha CS-80; the Yamaha GS-1 is responsible for the kalimba-like ostinato, not the solo.
